sections.summary: A flow chart links the design strategy (proposed structure, geology, existing information) to geotechnical investigations and design, then execution of works and exploitation, with reports at each stage.
sections.body: A flow chart: the strategy for geotechnical design (proposed structure, geology, existing information and experience; EC7 Parts 1-2) leads to geotechnical investigations (planning and re-evaluation of the programme; geology to a geological model; field and laboratory investigations to test results; reporting in the ground investigation report) and to design (evaluation of geotechnical parameters and coefficients, EC7 parts 1 and 2, giving the geotechnical model; geotechnical and structural design and specifications, EC7 part 1, giving the geotechnical design report, the final design report and the programme for inspection, supervision and monitoring). A call for bids leads to execution of works (execution studies and project; inspection, supervision and monitoring during construction with its report), then reception of the structure and exploitation (inspection and monitoring for maintenance with its report). sections.title: examples of recommendations for the spacing and depth of investigations
sections.summary: Guidance spacing of investigation points (15 m to 40 m grid for high-rise, up to 60 m for large-area, 20 m to 200 m for linear structures, two to six per special foundation, 25 m to 75 m for dams) and depths za below the lowest foundation point for each structure type, the largest applying, greater in weak ground.
sections.body: (1) Guidance spacing: high-rise and industrial structures, a grid at 15 m to 40 m; large-area structures, a grid at not more than 60 m; linear structures (roads, railways, channels, pipelines, dikes, tunnels, retaining walls), 20 m to 200 m; special structures (e.g. bridges, stacks, machinery foundations), two to six points per foundation; dams and weirs, 25 m to 75 m along relevant sections. (2) Guidance depth za is measured from the lowest point of the foundation or structural element, or the excavation base; where alternatives are given, the largest za applies. NOTE: for very large or complex projects some points generally go deeper than B.3 (5) to B.3 (13). (3) Go deeper where unfavourable geology, such as weak or compressible strata below stronger strata, is presumed. (4) Where structures under B.3 (5) to (8) and (13) stand on competent strata, za can drop to 2 m unless the geology is indistinct, when at least one borehole reaches za = 5 m; bedrock met at the proposed base becomes the reference level, otherwise za refers to the bedrock surface. (5) High-rise structures and civil engineering projects, the larger of za ≥ 6 m and za ≥ 3,0bF, bF the smaller side of the foundation (Figure B.1 a)). (6) Rafts and several foundation elements whose effects superimpose at depth: za ≥ 1,5·bB, bB the smaller side of the structure (Figure B.1 b)) (p. 104). (7) Embankments and cuttings, the larger of (Figure B.2): a) dams, 0,8h < za < 1,2h and za ≥ 6 m, h the embankment height; b) cuttings, za ≥ 2,0 m and za ≥ 0,4h, h printed as the dam height or depth of cutting (p. 105). (8) Linear structures, the larger of (Figure B.3): a) roads and airfields, za ≥ 2 m below the proposed formation level; b) trenches and pipelines, za ≥ 2 m below the invert level and za ≥ 1,5bAh, bAh the excavation width; c) embankment and cutting recommendations where relevant. (9) Small tunnels and caverns (Figure B.4): bAb < za < 2,0bAb, bAb the excavation width, also allowing for the groundwater of (10) b). (10) Excavations (Figure B.5) (p. 106): a) piezometric surface and groundwater below the excavation base, the larger of za ≥ 0,4h and za ≥ (t + 2,0) m, t the embedded length of the support and h the excavation depth; b) above the base, the larger of za ≥ (1,0H + 2,0) m and za ≥ (t + 2,0) m, H the groundwater height above the base; if no low-permeability stratum is met down to these depths, za ≥ t + 5 m. (11) Water-retaining structures: za set by the impounded water level, hydrogeology and construction method. (12) Cut-off walls (Figure B.6): za ≥ 2 m below the surface of the stratum impermeable to groundwater (p. 107). (13) Piles (Figure B.7), all three: za ≥ 1,0bg, za ≥ 5,0 m, za ≥ 3DF, DF the pile base diameter and bg the smaller side of the rectangle circumscribing the pile group at pile base level (p. 108). (pp. 104 to 108)

sections.title: Example of groundwater pressure derivations based on a model and long term measurements
sections.summary: Groundwater pressure is part of the hydrological cycle; a site model compiles hydrogeological information against measurements, and short site records can be extended with long-term records in a similar aquifer: statistics gave pressures within a few kPa from 15 years of reference data and 3 months on site.
sections.body: (1) Natural groundwater pressure is part of the hydrological cycle, influenced by precipitation, evapotranspiration, snow melt, surface run-off etc. (2) To model the groundwater at a site and its surroundings, available hydrogeological information should be compiled and compared with measurements: water level fluctuations, geohydrological maps, previous nearby measurements, typical levels of surface water or in wells, long term measurements in similar aquifers. (3) Project measurements are usually a short series, so the expected pressure for the design situation should be predicted from the model and long term measurements in a similar aquifer in the same region, combined with the short site record. (4) Statistical methods predicted groundwater pressure within a few kPa from 15 years of measurements in a reference system and a 3 month period on site (Figure C.1). (5) A conceptual model driven by precipitation and air temperature, calibrated against long term regional records, can also simulate the fluctuations. NOTE: see X.2 (p. 109). Figure C.1 shows A) a reference pipe with maximum and minimum levels over 15 years and the levels in the same year as the site readings, and B) the prediction pipe on the site with predicted maximum and minimum levels and the values measured from t0 to t1 (p. 110). (pp. 109 to 110)

sections.title: Example of a method to determine the settlement for spread foundations
sections.summary: A semi-empirical settlement method for spread foundations in coarse soil: E' = 2,5 qc (axisymmetric) or 3,5 qc (strip); s = C1 × C2 × (q - σ'v0) × ∫ Iz/(C3 × E') dz, C1 = 1 - 0,5[σ'v0/(q - σ'v0)], C2 = 1,2 + 0,2 lg t, C3 1,25 square or 1,75 strip (L > 10B); Iz from Figure D.1 (Schmertmann).
sections.body: (1) A semi-empirical method for settlement of spread foundations in coarse soil, with E' from qc: E' = 2,5 qc for axisymmetric (circular and square) and E' = 3,5 qc for plane strain (strip) foundations. (2) Settlement s under load pressure q: s = C1 × C2 × (q - σ'v0) × ∫ from 0 to zi of Iz/(C3 × E') dz, where C1 is 1 - 0,5 × [σ'v0/(q - σ'v0)]; C2 is 1,2 + 0,2 × lg t (t is not defined in the print); C3, the shape correction, is 1,25 for square and 1,75 for strip foundations with L > 10B; σ'v0 is the initial effective vertical stress at foundation level; zi is the depth influenced by the foundation pressure and width, in m; Iz is the strain influence factor. (3) Figure D.1 gives the Iz distribution for axisymmetric and plane strain foundations. NOTE 1: qc from an electrical cone. NOTE 2: published by Schmertmann (1970) and Schmertmann et al (1978); see X.3.1 (p. 112). In Figure D.1, Iz runs from 0,1 at the base to the peak Izp = 0,5 + 0,1 √((q - σ'v0)/σ'vp) at B/2 and to zero at 2B for axisymmetric footings (L/B = 1), and from 0,2 to Izp at B and to zero at 4B for plane strain (L/B > 10), σ'vp at the depth of Izp (p. 113). (pp. 112 to 113)

sections.title: Example of a method to determine the compressive resistance of a single pile
sections.summary: Maximum compressive resistance of a single pile from electrical CPT qc: Fmax = Fmax;base + Fmax;shaft, base pmax;base = 0,5 αp β s {(qc;I;mean + qc;II;mean)/2 + qc;III;mean} ≤ 15 MPa over the critical depth 0,7Deq to 4Deq, shaft pmax;shaft;z = αs × qc;z;a with cut-offs at 12 and 15 MPa; αp, αs from Tables D.5 and D.6, β from Figure D.3 (NEN 6743-1).
sections.body: (1) Maximum bearing resistance of a single pile from electrical CPT qc; reduce qc for over consolidation or excavation after the CPT. (2) Fmax = Fmax;base + Fmax;shaft, Fmax;base = Abase × pmax;base and Fmax;shaft = Cp ∫ from 0 to ΔL of pmax;shaft;z dz, where Abase is the base area (m2), Cp the shaft circumference in the layer holding the base (m), forces in MN, unit resistances in MPa, ΔL the distance from the base to the bottom of the first layer above it with qc < 2 MPa (and ΔL ≤ the enlarged point length if any), z depth positive downwards, Deq the equivalent base diameter (p. 116), Deq = 1,13 × a √(b/a), a the smaller and b the larger side (m), b ≤ 1,5 × a. (3) pmax;base = 0,5 αp β s {(qc;I;mean + qc;II;mean)/2 + qc;III;mean} with pmax;base ≤ 15 MPa: αp the pile class factor (Table D.5); β the pile point shape factor, interpolated in Figure D.3; s = (1 + sin φ'/r)/(1 + sin φ'), r = L/B of a rectangular point; qc;I;mean the mean qc;I from the base down to dcrit, 0,7Deq < dcrit < 4Deq, the critical depth giving the minimum pmax;base; qc;II;mean the mean of the lowest qc;II going up from dcrit to the base (p. 117); qc;III;mean the mean qc;III from the base up 8Deq (or 8 × a where b > 1,5 × a), starting from the lowest qc;II used; for continuous flight auger piles qc;III;mean cannot exceed 2 MPa unless CPTs within 1 m of the pile after fabrication are used. sections.summary: SPT blow count and density index: N60/ID² = a + bσ'v0 (σ'v0 in kPa × 10^-2), Table F.1 gives (N1)60 0-3 very loose to 42-58 very dense against ID 0 % to 100 %; fine sands × 55/60, coarse × 65/60; ageing raises a (Table F.2); over-consolidation multiplies b by (1 + 2K0)/(1 + 2K0NC) (Skempton 1986).
sections.body: (1) Examples of correlations of blow counts and density indices. (2) The blow count N60, density index ID = (emax - e)/(emax - emin) and effective total (initial) stress σ'v0 (kPa × 10^-2, wording as printed) in a given sand can be represented by N60/ID² = a + bσ'v0; a and b are nearly constant in normally consolidated sands for 0,35 < ID < 0,85 and 0,5 < σ'v0 < 2,5 in kPa × 10^-2 (Skempton 1986, Table 8). (3) For normally consolidated natural sand deposits Table F.1 correlates the normalised blow count (N1)60 with ID. (4) For fine sands reduce N-values in the ratio 55:60; for coarse sands increase them in the ratio 65:60. (5) Sand resists deformation more the longer it has consolidated; this ageing shows as higher blow counts and appears to raise a; Table F.2 gives typical results for normally consolidated fine sands (p. 125). (6) Over-consolidation increases b by the factor (1 + 2 × K0)/(1 + 2 × K0NC), K0 and K0NC the in-situ ratios of horizontal to vertical effective stress for the over-consolidated and normally-consolidated sand. (7) These correlations are for predominantly silica sands; in more crushable and compressible sands, such as calcareous sands or silica sands with a non-negligible amount of fines, they may underestimate ID. NOTE: published by Skempton (1986); see X.3.3 (p. 126). (pp. 125 to 126)

sections.title: Example of a method to calculate the settlement of spread foundations
sections.summary: Burland and Burbridge empirical settlement of spread foundations in granular soil: immediate settlement si (mm) of a square footing of width B (m) from Icc = 1,71/N̄^1,4 with B^0.7 and σ'p, N̄ the mean N over z1 = B^0,75; shape factor fs = [1,25(L/B)/(L/B + 0,25)]² and time factor ft = (1 + R3 + Rt lg t/3).
sections.body: (1) An empirical direct method for settlement of spread foundations in granular soil. (2) Settlement for stresses below the over consolidation pressure is taken as 1/3 of that for normally consolidated sand. The immediate settlement si (mm) of a square footing of width B (m) on over consolidated sand, if q' ≥ σ'p, is si = σ'p × B^0.7 × Icc/3 + (q' - σ'p) × B^0.7 × Icc (p. 126), where σ'p is the maximum previous overburden pressure (kPa); q' the average effective foundation pressure (kPa); Icc = af/B^0,7; af the foundation subgrade compressibility Δsi/Δq' (mm/kPa). If q' ≤ σ'p the equation becomes si = σ'p × B^0.7 × Icc/3 (as printed); for normally consolidated sands si = (q' - σ'p) × B^0.7 × Icc. (3) Regression of settlement records gives Icc = 1,71/N̄^1,4, N̄ the average SPT blow count over the depth of influence; the standard error of af runs from about 1,5 for N̄ > 25 to 1,8 for N̄ < about 10. (4) N is not corrected for overburden pressure and no energy ratio Er is stated; the water table is taken as already reflected in the blow count, but N' = 15 + 0,5 × (N - 15) should be applied to submerged fine or silty sands for N > 15; for gravels or sandy gravels increase N by a factor of about 1,25. (5) N̄ is the arithmetic mean of measured N over the depth of influence z1 = B^0,75, within which 75 % of the settlement occurs where N increases or is constant with depth; where N consistently decreases with depth, take 2B or the bottom of the soft layer, whichever is less. (6) Apply fs = [1,25 × (L/B)/(L/B + 0,25)]², which tends to 1,56 as L/B tends to infinity; no depth correction is needed for D/B < 3 (p. 127). (7) For time-dependent settlement in sands and gravels apply ft = (1 + R3 + Rt lg t/3) to the immediate settlement, ft for t ≥ 3 years, R3 the time-dependent factor for the first 3 years after construction and Rt that for each log cycle of time after 3 years. (8) For static loads conservative R3 and Rt are 0,3 and 0,2, so ft = 1,5 at t = 30 years; for fluctuating loads (tall chimneys, bridges, silos, turbines etc.) 0,7 and 0,8, so ft = 2,5 at t = 30 years. NOTE: published by Burland and Burbridge (1985); see X.3.3 (p. 128). (pp. 126 to 128)

sections.title: Example of establishing the stress-dependent oedometer modulus from DP results
sections.summary: Stress-dependent Eoed = w1 pa ((σ'v + 0,5Δσ'v)/pa)^w2 from DP results: poorly-graded sands above groundwater w1 = 214 lg N10L + 71 (4 ≤ N10L ≤ 50) or 249 lg N10H + 161 (3 ≤ N10H ≤ 10); stiff low-plasticity clays w1 = 4N10L + 30 (6 ≤ N10L ≤ 19) or 6N10H + 50 (3 ≤ N10H ≤ 13).
sections.body: (1) The vertical stress dependent oedometer modulus for spread foundation settlement is Eoed = w1 pa ((σ'v + 0,5 Δσ'v)/pa)^w2, w1 the stiffness coefficient; w2 the stiffness exponent, 0,5 for sands with CU ≤ 3 and 0,6 for clays of low plasticity (Ip ≤ 10; wL ≤ 35); σ'v the effective vertical stress from overburden at or below the foundation base; Δσ'v that caused by the structure; pa atmospheric pressure; Ip plasticity index; wL liquid limit. (2) w1 from DP tests by soil type: poorly-graded sands (CU ≤ 3) above groundwater, w1 = 214 lg N10L + 71 (DPL; 4 ≤ N10L ≤ 50) and w1 = 249 lg N10H + 161 (DPH; 3 ≤ N10H ≤ 10); low-plasticity clays of at least stiff consistency (0,75 ≤ Ic ≤ 1,30) above groundwater, Ic the consistency index, w1 = 4N10L + 30 (DPL; 6 ≤ N10L ≤ 19) and w1 = 6N10H + 50 (DPH; 3 ≤ N10H ≤ 13). NOTE: published by Stenzel et al. (1978) and Biedermann (1984) and in DIN 4094-3:2002; see X.3.4. (p. 130)

sections.title: Weight sounding test (WST)
sections.summary: Table H.1 estimates φ' and drained E' of naturally deposited quartz and feldspar sands from mean weight sounding resistance in a layer (Swedish experience): very loose 0-10 half-turns/0,2 m, φ' 29-32°, E' < 10 MPa to very dense > 80, 40-42°, 60-90 MPa; use the lower value of each interval when only WST results exist.
sections.body: (1) An example of φ' and drained Young's modulus E' estimated from weight sounding resistance on Swedish experience, correlating the mean resistance in a layer with mean φ' and E' (Table H.1). (2) If only weight sounding results are available, select the lower value of each interval of φ' and E' in Table H.1. (3) Disregard peak values caused for example by stones or pebbles, common in weight sounding in gravel. NOTE: published by Bergdahl et al. (1993); see X.3.5. (p. 132)
key_points: φ' and E' of quartz and feldspar sands from WST resistance (p. 132).
Silty soil: divide WST resistance by 1,3 first (p. 132).
Only WST results: take the lower value of each interval (p. 132).
Ignore peaks from stones or pebbles (p. 132).
tables: Table H.1: Values of the effective angle of shearing resistance (φ') and drained Young's modulus of elasticity (E') for naturally deposited quartz and feldspar sands estimated from weight sounding resistance in Sweden - density index; weight sounding resistance a), half-turns/0,2 m; φ' b), °; E' c), MPa: very loose 0-10, 29-32, < 10; loose 10-30, 32-35, 10-20; medium dense 20-50, 35-37, 20-30; dense 40-90, 37-40, 30-60; very dense > 80, 40-42, 60-90 (overlapping ranges as printed). a) In silty soil divide the resistance by 1,3 before determining the relative density. b) Valid for sands; reduce by 3° for silty soil; 2° may be added for gravels. c) E' approximates the stress and time-dependent secant modulus for settlements after 10 years with a 2:1 vertical stress distribution; values can be 50 % lower in silty soil and 50 % higher in gravelly soil, considerably higher in over-consolidated coarse soil; for ground pressure above 2/3 of the ULS design pressure use half the tabulated modulus (p. 132)
sections.applicability: The standard's example derived-value correlation for the weight sounding test, feeding bearing-resistance and settlement analytical methods.

sections.title: Field vane test (FVT)
sections.summary: Heading for Annex I, field vane test (FVT): examples for the correction factor μ applied to the field vane strength cfv, from Atterberg limits and the state of consolidation (I.1 to I.5).
sections.body: Annex I (informative) heading for I.1 to I.5; it has no text of its own. (p. 133)
key_points: See I.1 to I.5 (p. 133).
sections.applicability: Correcting field vane shear strength to undrained shear strength with a correction factor μ (EN 1997-2 Annex I examples).

sections.title: Examples of procedures to determine correction factors for the undrained shear strength
sections.summary: Field vane results are corrected to undrained shear strength by cu = μ × cfv, μ from the procedures of I.2 to I.5, based mainly on back-analysis of embankment failures and load tests in soft clays; choose by local experience in the clay type and remember the drained strength may be lower.
sections.body: (1) Procedures for correction factors of field vane results to obtain cu from the measured cfv are given in I.2 to I.5; they rest mainly on back-analysis of embankment failures and load tests in soft clays, and all give a correction factor μ used in cu = μ × cfv, cfv the undrained shear strength measured in the field vane test. (2) Base the procedure on local experience in the actual type of clay; consider also that the drained shear strength might be lower than the undrained. NOTE: see X.3.6. (p. 133)
key_points: cu = μ × cfv (p. 133).
Factors from back-analysis of embankment failures and load tests in soft clays (p. 133).
Drained strength might be lower than undrained (p. 133).
sections.applicability: Graphical routes to the FVT correction factor mu, an alternative to the closed-form I.5 equations when charts/local calibration are preferred.

sections.title: Example of the determination of the correction factor μ based on Atterberg limits
sections.summary: For soft normally-consolidated clays μ is linked to the liquid limit or plasticity index (sample curve of μ against wL in Figure I.1); μ above 1,2 needs supplementary investigations and fissured clays may need μ as low as 0,3 or other methods such as plate load tests.
sections.body: (1) For soft, normally-consolidated clays μ is linked to the liquid limit or the plasticity index; Figure I.1 gives a sample curve. (2) Do not use μ greater than 1,2 without support from supplementary investigations. (3) Fissured clays can need μ as low as 0,3; there cu should be determined by methods other than field vane tests, e.g. plate load tests. NOTE: the Danish Geotechnical Institute (1959) gives examples for fissured clays; see X.3.6 (p. 133). Figure I.1 (Larsson et al. 1984) plots μ against wL for normally consolidated clays; Figure I.2 plots μ against cfv/σ'v0 for Ip < 40 % and Ip > 40 % in over-consolidated clays, with cu = μ × cfv and μ ≤ 1 (p. 134). (pp. 133 to 134)
key_points: Figure I.1: μ against liquid limit, NC clays (p. 134).
μ > 1,2 only with supplementary investigations (p. 133).
Fissured clays: μ as low as 0,3; prefer plate load tests (p. 133).
figures: Figure I.1: An example of correction factors for cfv based on the liquid limit for normally consolidated clays - μ (0,4 to 1,2) against wL (0 to 200 %) (p. 134)

Figure I.2: Examples of correction factors for cfv based on plasticity index and effective vertical stress (σ'v0) for over-consolidated clays - μ against cfv/σ'v0 (0 to 0,6), curves for Ip < 40 % and Ip > 40 %; cu = μ × cfv, μ ≤ 1 (p. 134)
sections.applicability: Graphical routes to the FVT correction factor mu, an alternative to the closed-form I.5 equations when charts/local calibration are preferred.

sections.title: Example of the determination of the correction factor μ on Atterberg limits and the state of consolidation
sections.summary: This correction links μ to plasticity index Ip and effective vertical stress σ'v0, with sample curves in Figure I.2 (Aas 1979).
sections.body: (1) This correction is linked to the plasticity index Ip and the effective vertical stress σ'v0 in the ground; Figure I.2 presents sample curves (p. 134). NOTE: Figure I.2 was published by Aas (1979); see X.3.6 (p. 135). (pp. 134 to 135)
key_points: μ from Ip and cfv/σ'v0, Figure I.2 (p. 134).
sections.applicability: Field vane correction factor μ from plasticity index and effective vertical stress, with the curves of Figure I.2 (EN 1997-2 Annex I.3).

sections.title: Example of the determination of the correction factor μ based on Atterberg limits and state of consolidation
sections.summary: To allow for over-consolidation, Figure I.3 separates normally-consolidated clays (between the 'young' and 'aged' curves of cfv/σ'v0 against Ip) from over-consolidated ones (above 'aged'); Figure I.4 then gives μ against cfv/σ'v0 on its NC or OC curve (Aas et al. 1986).
sections.body: (1) This procedure allows for over-consolidation. (2) First estimate whether the clay is over-consolidated from Figure I.3, the quotient cfv/σ'v0 against Ip: clays between the 'young' and 'aged' curves are normally-consolidated (NC), clays above 'aged' over-consolidated (OC). (3) Correct NC soils by the curve marked NC in Figure I.4 and OC soils by the curve marked OC (p. 135). Figure I.3 plots cfv/σ'v0 (0 to 1,2) against Ip (0 to 120 %), with curves of ROC = σ'p/σ'v0 1 to 6, the curve of Figure I.2, the lower limit of young clay, the upper limit of young clay and lower limit of aged clay, and the NC and OC ranges; NOTE: published by Aas et al. (1986); see X.3.6 (p. 135). Figure I.4 plots μ (0,2 to 1,4) against cfv/σ'v0 (0 to 1) for NC and OC clays; NOTE: see X.3.6 (p. 136). (pp. 135 to 136)
key_points: Figure I.3 sorts NC and OC clays by cfv/σ'v0 and Ip (p. 135).
Between 'young' and 'aged' curves: NC; above 'aged': OC (p. 135).
Figure I.4 gives μ on the NC or OC curve (p. 136).
figures: Figure I.3: Diagram for separating normally-consolidated and over-consolidated clays - cfv/σ'v0 against Ip (%), ROC = σ'p/σ'v0 curves 1 to 6; key: 1 curve of Fig. I.2, 2 lower limit of young clay, 3 upper limit of young clay and lower limit of aged clay, 4 range of NC clays, 5 range of OC clays (p. 135)
Figure I.4: Correction factors for normally-consolidated and over-consolidated clays - μ against cfv/σ'v0, 1 NC, 2 OC (p. 136)
sections.applicability: Field vane correction factor μ allowing for over-consolidation: separating NC from OC clays (Figure I.3) and reading μ (Figure I.4) (EN 1997-2 Annex I.4).

sections.title: Example of the determination of the correction factor μ based on Atterberg limits and the state of consolidation
sections.summary: Closed-form μ (Larsson and Åhnberg 2003): μ = (0,43/wL)^0,45 ≥ 0,5 for NC and slightly OC clays; × (ROC/1,3)^-0,15 where ROC > 1,3; with ROC unknown, cfv = 0,45 × wL × σ'p (Hansbo 1957) gives μ = (0,43/wL)^0,45 × (cfv/(0,585wL × σ'v0))^-0,15.
sections.body: (1) This procedure also allows for over-consolidation. (2) For normally-consolidated and slightly over-consolidated clays μ = (0,43/wL)^0,45 ≥ 0,5, wL the liquid limit (see Figure I.1). (3) Where the over-consolidation ratio exceeds 1,3, μ = (0,43/wL)^0,45 × (ROC/1,3)^-0,15 (AC1), ROC the over-consolidation ratio. NOTE: from Larsson and Åhnberg (2003); see X.3.6 (p. 136). (4) If ROC is not determined it can be estimated from cfv = 0,45 × wL × σ'p, giving μ = (0,43/wL)^0,45 × (cfv/(0,585wL × σ'v0))^-0,15 (AC1). NOTE: the relation, printed there as cfv = 0,45 × wl × σ'p, stems from Hansbo (1957); see X.3.6 (p. 137). (pp. 136 to 137)
key_points: cfv = 0,45 × wL × σ'p (Hansbo 1957) (p. 137).
sections.applicability: Closed-form determination of the FVT correction factor mu feeding Eq 4.4 (cu=mu*cfv), the preferred route when wL and (optionally) OCR are known.

sections.title: Flat dilatometer test (DMT)
sections.summary: Eoed = dσ'/dε from DMT: Eoed = RM × EDMT, RM from local experience or from IDMT and KDMT: RM = 0,14 + 2,36 lg KDMT (IDMT ≤ 0,6); RM0 + (2,5 - RM0) lg KDMT, RM0 = 0,14 + 0,15(IDMT - 0,6) (0,6 < IDMT < 3,0); 0,5 + 2 lg KDMT (IDMT ≥ 3); 0,32 + 2,18 lg KDMT (KDMT > 10); RM at least 0,85 (Marchetti 2001).
sections.body: (1) An example of correlations between Eoed and DMT results, for the one-dimensional tangent modulus Eoed = dσ'/dε: Eoed = RM × EDMT, with RM from local experience or from: if IDMT ≤ 0,6, RM = 0,14 + 2,36 lg KDMT; if 0,6 < IDMT < 3,0, RM = RM0 + (2,5 - RM0) lg KDMT with RM0 = 0,14 + 0,15 (IDMT - 0,6); if IDMT ≥ 3, RM = 0,5 + 2 lg KDMT (AC1); if KDMT > 10, RM = 0,32 + 2,18 lg KDMT; where these give RM < 0,85, take RM = 0,85. IDMT is the material index and KDMT the horizontal stress index from the flat dilatometer test. NOTE: published by Marchetti (2001); see X.3.7. (p. 138)
key_points: Eoed = RM × EDMT (p. 138).
IDMT ≥ 3: RM = 0,5 + 2 lg KDMT; KDMT > 10: RM = 0,32 + 2,18 lg KDMT (p. 138).
RM not less than 0,85 (p. 138).

equations.description: Eoed = RM × EDMT; RM = 0,14 + 2,36 lg KDMT (IDMT ≤ 0,6); RM = RM0 + (2,5 - RM0) lg KDMT, RM0 = 0,14 + 0,15 (IDMT - 0,6) (0,6 < IDMT < 3,0); RM = 0,5 + 2 lg KDMT (IDMT ≥ 3); RM = 0,32 + 2,18 lg KDMT (KDMT > 10); RM < 0,85 taken as 0,85 (p. 138)

sections.applicability: The standard's sole DMT-derived-value annex; supports the settlement-by-adjusted-elasticity method referenced from 4.10.4.1(3).

sections.title: Plate loading test (PLT)
sections.summary: Heading for Annex K, plate loading test (PLT): examples for cu (K.1), plate settlement modulus EPLT (K.2), coefficient of sub-grade reaction ks (K.3) and footing settlement in sand (K.4).
sections.body: Annex K (informative) heading for K.1 to K.4; it has no text of its own. (p. 139)
key_points: See K.1 to K.4 (p. 139).
sections.applicability: Undrained shear strength, plate settlement modulus, sub-grade reaction and footing settlement in sand from plate loading tests (EN 1997-2 Annex K examples).

sections.title: Example of deriving the value of undrained shear strength
sections.summary: cu from the PLT: cu = (pu - (γ × z))/Nc, pu the ultimate contact pressure, γ × z the total stress at test level in a borehole narrower than three plate diameters, Nc = 6 for circular plates on the subsoil surface and 9 in boreholes deeper than four plate diameters (Marsland 1972).
sections.body: (1) cu from the PLT: cu = (pu - (γ × z))/Nc, where pu is the ultimate contact pressure from the PLT; γ × z the total stress (density times depth) at test level when the test is in a borehole of diameter smaller than three times the plate diameter or width; Nc the bearing capacity factor, for circular plates Nc = 6 (typically for PLT on the subsoil surface) and Nc = 9 (typically for PLT in boreholes deeper than four times the plate diameter or width). NOTE: published by Marsland (1972); see X.3.8. (p. 139)
key_points: Nc = 6 on the subsoil surface; 9 in boreholes deeper than 4 plate diameters (p. 139).

equations.description: cu = (pu - (γ × z))/Nc; circular plates Nc = 6 (PLT on the subsoil surface) or Nc = 9 (PLT in boreholes deeper than four times the plate diameter or width) (p. 139)

sections.applicability: PLT-based undrained shear strength determination, feeding the analytical bearing-resistance method of 4.11.4(4).

sections.title: Example of deriving the value of the plate settlement modulus
sections.summary: Plate settlement (secant) modulus: EPLT = Δp/Δs × πb/4 × (1 - ν²) at ground level or in an excavation at least five plate diameters wide, × Cz at the base of a borehole (Figure K.1, Burland 1969); ν = 0,5 undrained in fine soil and 0,3 in coarse soil if not otherwise determined.
sections.body: (1) An example of deriving the plate settlement modulus EPLT (secant modulus). (2) For tests at ground level or in an excavation whose bottom width or diameter is at least five times the plate diameter, EPLT = Δp/Δs × πb/4 × (1 - ν²), Δp the selected range of applied contact pressure; Δs the change in total settlement, including creep, for Δp; b the plate diameter; ν Poisson's ratio for the test conditions. (3) If not otherwise determined, ν = 0,5 for undrained conditions in fine soil and 0,3 for coarse soil (p. 139). (4) At the base of a borehole EPLT = Δp/Δs × πb/4 × (1 - ν²)Cz, Cz a depth correction factor, the ratio of the depth load to settlement of the corresponding surface load, with suggested values in Figure K.1. NOTE: published by Burland (1969); see X.3.8 (p. 140). (pp. 139 to 140)
key_points: EPLT = Δp/Δs × πb/4 × (1 - ν²) (p. 139).
Excavation at least five plate diameters wide (p. 139).
ν = 0,5 undrained fine soil, 0,3 coarse soil (p. 139).
Borehole base: × Cz from Figure K.1 (p. 140).

equations.description: EPLT = Δp/Δs × πb/4 × (1 - ν²) at ground level or in a wide excavation (p. 139); EPLT = Δp/Δs × πb/4 × (1 - ν²)Cz at the base of a borehole (p. 140); ν = 0,5 undrained fine soil, 0,3 coarse soil if not otherwise determined

figures: Figure K.1: Depth correction factor Cz as a function of plate diameter b and depth z for PLT results obtained with a uniform circular load at the base of an unlined shaft - Cz (0,5 to 1) against z/b (0 to 20) for ν = 0,49, 0,25 and 0,0 (p. 140)
sections.applicability: PLT-based deformation modulus determination, feeding the adjusted-elasticity settlement method of 4.11.4(5).

sections.title: Example of deriving the value of coefficient of sub-grade reaction
sections.summary: Coefficient of sub-grade reaction ks = Δp/Δs from the PLT, Δs including creep, stating the loading plate dimensions (Bergdahl 1993).
sections.body: (1) ks = Δp/Δs, Δp the selected range of applied contact pressure and Δs the change in settlement, including creep, for Δp. (2) State the loading plate dimensions when calculating ks. NOTE: published by Bergdahl (1993); see X.3.8. (p. 140)
key_points: ks = Δp/Δs (p. 140).
State the plate dimensions with ks (p. 140).

equations.description: ks = Δp/Δs, Δs including creep settlements; state the loading plate dimensions (p. 140)

sections.applicability: PLT-based coefficient of sub-grade reaction for deformation-evaluation methods (e.g. beam-on-elastic-foundation analysis).

sections.title: Example of a method to calculate the settlement of spread foundations in sand
sections.summary: Footing settlement in sand directly from a PLT: Figure K.3 scales the plate settlement s1 to the footing settlement s by the width ratio b/b1 for loose, medium dense and dense sand, if the ground to more than twice the width below the footing matches that below the plate (Figure K.2; Bergdahl et al 1993).
sections.body: (1) Figure K.3 gives a footing's settlement in sand empirically, provided the soil under the footing, down to more than twice its width, matches the soil under the plate (Figure K.2) (p. 141). Figure K.2 shows the test plate of width b1 with settlement s1 and the footing of width b with predicted settlement s, each with its influenced zone, p the load (p. 141). Figure K.3 plots s/s1 against b/b1 (1 to 200) for 1 loose, 2 medium dense and 3 dense sand. NOTE: published by Bergdahl et al (1993); see X.3.8 (p. 142). (pp. 141 to 142)
key_points: Valid if ground to twice the width below the footing matches that below the plate (p. 141).
s/s1 against b/b1 for loose, medium dense, dense sand (p. 142).
figures: Figure K.2: Influenced area beneath a test plate and a footing - plate width b1, settlement s1; footing width b, predicted settlement s; load p; influenced zones (p. 141)
Figure K.3: Graph for calculations of settlement based on plate loading tests - s/s1 against b/b1, 1 loose, 2 medium dense, 3 dense (p. 142)
sections.applicability: Direct-design empirical settlement scaling from small-plate PLT results to a full-size footing on sand.
